1.pericope_label: So when David was old and full of days, he made Solomon his son king over Israel. And he gathered together all the princes of Israel, with the priests and the Levites. Now the Levites were numbered from the age of thirty years and upward: and their number by their polls, man by man, was thirty and eight thousand. Of which, twenty and four thousand were to set forward the work of the house of the Lord; and six thousand were officers and judges: Moreover four thousand were porters; and four thousand praised the Lord with the instruments which I made, said David, to praise therewith. And David divided them into courses among the sons of Levi, namely, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the accession formula literally, explains the brevity of the notice as the chronicler declining to handle David's family affairs, treats the princes, priests and Levites as the three estates of the realm, and argues with Delitzsch that verses 4 and 5 are a spoken decree of David; Delitzsch defends the same punctuation and attacks the age of thirty in verse 3 as improbable against verse 24.
Gill sets David in the last year of his age and notes that the Levites were first numbered as in the days of Moses.

Clarke and Wesley both explain the missing upper age-limit by the ceasing of the burdens, the ark being fixed; Clarke further denies that David had any positive divine authority for these arrangements and reads Amos as condemning the instruments David made.

Henry reads the coronation politically, supplies the narrative the chronicler omits, contrasts 8,580 serviceable Levites in the wilderness with 38,000 now, and defends this census as free of the pride that marred the earlier one.

debates: Whether the age of thirty in verse 3 can stand beside the twenty of verse 24, and whether the wilderness upper limit of fifty still applied.

Whether David's musical establishment had divine authority: Ellicott cites Amos 6:5 as evidence that David invented stringed instruments, while Clarke cites the same verse as a condemnation of them and denies any positive warrant for the arrangement.
outliers: Henry and Ellicott independently hear "satisfied with days" in the phrase full of days, Ellicott adding the parallel of Horace's philosopher departing life like a satisfied guest.
themes: So when David was old and full of days, he made Solomon his son king over Israel.
And he gathered together all the princes of Israel, with the priests and the Levites.
Now the Levites were numbered from the age of thirty years and upward: and their number by their polls, man by man, was thirty and eight thousand.
Of which, twenty and four thousand were to set forward the work of the house of the Lord; and six thousand were officers and judges:
Moreover four thousand were porters; and four thousand praised the Lord with the instruments which I made, said David, to praise therewith.
And David divided them into courses among the sons of Levi, namely, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

7.pericope_label: Of the Gershonites were, Laadan, and Shimei. The sons of Laadan; the chief was Jehiel, and Zetham, and Joel, three. The sons of Shimei; Shelomith, and Haziel, and Haran, three. These were the chief of the fathers of Laadan. And the sons of Shimei were, Jahath, Zina, and Jeush, and Beriah. These four were the sons of Shimei. And Jahath was the chief, and Zizah the second: but Jeush and Beriah had not many sons; therefore they were in one reckoning, according to their father’s house. The sons of Kohath; Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, four. The sons of Amram; Aaron and Moses: and Aaron was separated, that he should sanctify the most holy things, he and his sons for ever, to burn incense before the Lord, to minister unto him, and to bless in his name for ever. Now concerning Moses the man of God, his sons were named of the tribe of Levi. The sons of Moses were, Gershom, and Eliezer. Of the sons of Gershom, Shebuel was the chief. And the sons of Eliezer were, Rehabiah the chief. And Eliezer had none other sons; but the sons of Rehabiah were very many. Of the sons of Izhar; Shelomith the chief. Of the sons of Hebron; Jeriah the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth. Of the sons of Uzziel; Michah the first, and Jesiah the second. The sons of Merari; Mahli, and Mushi. The sons of Mahli; Eleazar, and Kish. And Eleazar died, and had no sons, but daughters: and their brethren the sons of Kish took them. The sons of Mushi; Mahli, and Eder, and Jeremoth, three.

schools.summary: Ellicott treats the genealogy as an arithmetical problem, requiring twenty-four Levitical houses to match 24,000 men at a thousand to the class, and emends the second Mahli of verse 23 away to reach the figure, listing four objections to his own conjecture; Delitzsch sets out the tribe-family-house scheme and rejects the same emendation from the other side, calling the verses that supply Merari a third son arbitrary interpolations.
Gill, following Kimchi, keeps the two Shimeis of verses 9 and 10 distinct.
Clarke gives the merging of small houses a workload rationale and supplies the Targum's claim that the posterity of Rehabiah was multiplied on account of the merits of Moses.
Henry reads the levelling of Moses' line with the common Levites as the proof of his self-denial, and the elevation of Aaron's as the recompense of his submission.

debates: How many Merarite houses the register should yield, and whether the defect is met by emending verse 23 or by rejecting the later verses that supply a third son of Merari.
Why weak houses were merged: for the sake of the workload, for administrative tidiness, or, as Henry has it, so that those weak separately might appear considerable together.
outliers: Ellicott states the case against his own emendation at length, noting that all the old versions support the received text and that the two other lists of Merari's sons name only two.

24.pericope_label: These were the sons of Levi after the house of their fathers; even the chief of the fathers, as they were counted by number of names by their polls, that did the work for the service of the house of the Lord, from the age of twenty years and upward. For David said, The Lord God of Israel hath given rest unto his people, that they may dwell in Jerusalem for ever: And also unto the Levites; they shall no more carry the tabernacle, nor any vessels of it for the service thereof. For by the last words of David the Levites were numbered from twenty years old and above: Because their office was to wait on the sons of Aaron for the service of the house of the Lord, in the courts, and in the chambers, and in the purifying of all holy things, and the work of the service of the house of God; Both for the shewbread, and for the fine flour for meat offering, and for the unleavened cakes, and for that which is baked in the pan, and for that which is fried, and for all manner of measure and size; And to stand every morning to thank and praise the Lord, and likewise at even; And to offer all burnt sacrifices unto the Lord in the sabbaths, in the new moons, and on the set feasts, by number, according to the order commanded unto them, continually before the Lord: And that they should keep the charge of the tabernacle of the congregation, and the charge of the holy place, and the charge of the sons of Aaron their brethren, in the service of the house of the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott surveys four ways of handling the twenty against the thirty and settles on none, undercutting the favoured one by observing that twenty was in any case the military age; he confines the charge of measures to the sanctuary's own vessels, and joins Delitzsch in assigning the morning and evening thanksgiving to the singers rather than to the Levites at the altar.
Gill, on the Targum and Kimchi, has the Levites singing whenever burnt offerings were brought and some of them helping the priests to slay the sacrifices.

Clarke takes the two ages for two successive ordinances, the later being David's last orders; Wesley takes them for two simultaneous grades, twenty for preparation and instruction and thirty for full admission.

Henry supplies a disciplinary motive for the lower age, that idleness in the unemployed young Levites was a blemish and a hindrance, and reads the calling of the priests "their brethren" as a check on priestly pretension.

debates: How the twenty of verse 24 stands with the thirty of verse 3: a transcriptional error, two divergent sources, two successive decrees, two simultaneous grades, or a disciplinary reform.
Whether the Levites kept the national standards of weight and measure, as Clarke, Wesley and Henry hold, or only the measuring vessels of the sanctuary, as Ellicott argues.
Whether the morning and evening thanksgiving belonged to the singers alone or also to the Levites who prepared the sacrifices.
outliers: Clarke reports and dismisses as a conceit the tradition that the priests themselves sowed, ground and baked the grain for the shewbread.
themes: These were the sons of Levi after the house of their fathers; even the chief of the fathers, as they were counted by number of names by their polls, that did the work for the service of the house of the Lord, from the age of twenty years and upward.
For David said, The Lord God of Israel hath given rest unto his people, that they may dwell in Jerusalem for ever:
And also unto the Levites; they shall no more carry the tabernacle, nor any vessels of it for the service thereof.
For by the last words of David the Levites were numbered from twenty years old and above:

Because their office was to wait on the sons of Aaron for the service of the house of the Lord, in the courts, and in the chambers, and in the purifying of all holy things, and the work of the service of the house of God;

Both for the shewbread, and for the fine flour for meat offering, and for the unleavened cakes, and for that which is baked in the pan, and for that which is fried, and for all manner of measure and size;
And to stand every morning to thank and praise the Lord, and likewise at even;
And to offer all burnt sacrifices unto the Lord in the sabbaths, in the new moons, and on the set feasts, by number, according to the order commanded unto them, continually before the Lord:

And that they should keep the charge of the tabernacle of the congregation, and the charge of the holy place, and the charge of the sons of Aaron their brethren, in the service of the house of the Lord.
